title: Higher in the Air: Design of Snowboard Course

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF page 1 is the summary sheet, PDF page 2 is the title page, and PDF pages 3-23 contain the front matter and printed body pages 2-22.

context_sources.use: Official definition of vertical air and the required maximum-air, twist, and practical-course tasks.
Official designation of control 9159, Peking University, as an Outstanding Winner without a listed special award.

limitations: All 23 pages were rendered at 144 DPI and visually reviewed through contact sheets; central equations, response curves, sensitivity plots, 3D geometry, safety, and twist sections received full-resolution inspection.
Text extraction corrupts some mathematical glyphs, so all cited equation defects were verified against rendered pages.
No code, raw numerical data, convergence output, measured rider trajectory, or construction dataset accompanies the paper.
The official results establish Outstanding status but provide no judge commentary explaining the award.

required_outputs: Design a half-pipe shape that maximizes maximum vertical distance above the coping.
Tailor the design for another performance requirement such as twist.
Determine tradeoffs needed for a practical course.
paper_interpretation: Use final mechanical energy before the next jump as a proxy for vertical air.
Derive a curvature-dependent friction-energy ODE and study quarter-circle and quarter-ellipse path families.
Use a transformed 3D slice to choose a downhill slope that preserves hanging height across a trick.
Use qualitative safety, construction, and twist arguments to modify the theoretical geometry.
task_reconstruction.coverage_note: The paper gives a broad design narrative but never computes official vertical air through a flight model, never predicts twist, and does not quantify safety, construction, or tradeoff outcomes.

section_map.summary: Previews assumptions, energy ODE, circle and ellipse models, numerical sensitivity, 3D slope, and practical adjustments.
Provides detailed navigation, nineteen indexed figures, and the full section architecture.
Restates the three tasks and frames course design as gravitational influx versus collision and friction loss.
Defines geometry and energy symbols and motivates the mass-point, rigid-course, zero-speed, and inelastic-impact assumptions.
Builds the normal-force and energy-loss equations for a general cross-section.
Derives the energy ODE, collision initial energy, functional solution, and final-energy objective.
Restricts the functional problem to a circle and obtains a closed-form energy expression.
Shows circle sensitivity curves and begins the ellipse family.
States forward Euler and bisection methods and uses a no-collision ablation to expose a degenerate right-angle optimum.
Adds landing collision and then a linear air-resistance term.
Reports the 2D ellipse design and prints the sensitivity-coefficient definition.
Reports one-at-a-time sensitivities of a* to six inputs.
Introduces downhill distance and slope geometry.
Transforms the 3D course to a 2D slice and recomputes ellipse parameters.
Chooses 17.1 degrees by equal hanging heights and transitions to practical tradeoffs.
Discusses safety, construction, bottom width, edge angle, and twist qualitatively.
Self-assesses the model ladder, visual analysis, sensitivity, omitted athlete movement, out-of-plane paths, and ellipse restriction.
Reports a=4.42 m, b=5.4 m, and practical slope 17.5 degrees and claims agreement with real data.

contributions.summary: Connects path slope and curvature to Coulomb loss through normal loading in a dimensionally coherent energy equation.
Obtains a closed-form quarter-circle result before escalating to numerical ellipse optimization.
Removes collision to show that friction alone produces an unreasonable degenerate geometry.
Separately adds snow friction, collision, and aerodynamic resistance and compares their influence.
Uses six response curves and normalized coefficients to compare parameter influence.
Explicitly distinguishes theoretical energy efficiency from safety, construction, and rider-preparation needs.
Uses a clear model ladder, many response plots, and a candid limitations section to make an ambitious analysis accessible.

dependency_graph.state_model: collision initial energy -> Equation 5 energy ODE -> final energy Et
dependency_graph.optimization: circle radius or ellipse axes -> final-energy response -> reported R*, a*, b*
dependency_graph.decision: equal-height slope 17.1 degrees -> qualitative safety and construction adjustment -> final slope 17.5 degrees
missing_links: course shape and takeoff state -> airborne trajectory -> endogenous landing x0
takeoff direction and speed -> maximum vertical distance above coping
contact actuation -> angular impulse -> twist and landing
geometry -> impact load and injury risk
construction geometry -> snow stability, cost, and feasibility

assumptions.summary: Treats rider and board as a mass point constrained to the modeled surface.
Uses a perfectly rigid half-pipe, zero initial speed, constant snow friction, and perfectly inelastic instantaneous landing.
Initially limits losses to snow friction and collision, then promises an air-resistance correction.
Sets w=9 m, h0=5.4 m, mu=0.1, hi=9 m, and m=75 kg as representative values.
Assumes linear air resistance and a fixed 0.5 m^2 windward area.
Sets downhill travel per trick to about 20 m from course length and the number of tricks.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses International Ski Federation size ranges and a cited snow-friction range to set baseline geometry and mu.
Takes alpha=0.75 Ns/m^3 from a general Wind Scale Table rather than athlete drag measurements.
Converts a 100-150 m course and 6-7 tricks into a fixed approximately 20 m downhill distance per trick.
Provides six references but no raw course, rider, trajectory, aerodynamic, load, or validation dataset.

models.summary: General 2D mechanical-energy ODE with gravity, curvature-dependent normal force, Coulomb friction, and an inelastic landing initial condition.
Closed-form circle-family energy and one-dimensional radius optimization.
Forward-Euler energy propagation over a two-parameter ellipse family with stated bisection optimization.
Adds a linear alpha A v loss term to the energy ODE.
Uses local one-at-a-time elasticities for a* while b* remains fixed at the height boundary.
Maps a sloped 3D course slice into a modified 2D curve and reuses the energy model.
Uses cubic-spline interpolation of final hanging height versus slope and selects the equal-height intersection.

verification.summary: Provides an analytical special case that could check the numerical solver, though no numerical comparison is printed.
Uses a collision ablation to demonstrate qualitative mechanism necessity.
Uses an air-loss ablation to show geometry stability under the assumed linear drag law.
Explores local parameter response but omits joint uncertainty and decision reversals.
Interpolates a design point but supplies no raw values, convergence, interpolation error, or code.
Claims fit to real data after shifting the slope toward the cited real-world value; no independent external validation is performed.

results_trace.summary: Reports R*=3.831 m for hi=9 m, x0=0.5 m, mu=0.1, and w=9 m.
Reports (a*,b*)=(4.19,5.4) m; b*=h0 is the upper boundary.
Reports local coefficients for x0, hi, alpha, h0, mu, and Ei, including a negative initial-height coefficient that contradicts the prose.
Reports slope 17.1 degrees from equal hanging height and corresponding ellipse (4.42,5.4) m.
Changes slope to 17.5 degrees and edge angle to about 85 degrees using qualitative safety, standard, and construction arguments.
Concludes a=4.42 m, b=5.4 m, and slope 17.5 degrees without a direct vertical-air or twist output.

writing_logic.summary: Gives the complete modeling storyline and headline results before the body.
Moves from a general functional to a simple circle and then a more flexible ellipse.
Introduces snow friction, collision, and air loss one at a time to expose their effects.
Extends the 2D cross-section to downhill 3D geometry after completing the planar study.
Explicitly marks the transition from idealized analysis to safety, construction, and performance tradeoffs.
Ends with strengths and weaknesses before the conclusion, helping readers bound the claims.
Moves from energy baseline through circle, ellipse, sensitivity, 3D extension and practical tradeoffs in body order.
The general profile functional is deliberately reduced to circle and ellipse families, making the loss of generality explicit.
Equal-height slope selection precedes safety, construction and twist adjustments rather than being presented as the final answer.

language_observations.summary: Uses concise model-result sequencing and names important parameters, making the paper easy to triage.
Strong front matter gives a reader an immediate map of models, sensitivity, 3D analysis, and tradeoffs.
The predicted positive initial-height effect contradicts the negative plot and reported coefficient.
Openly admits ignored athlete movement, out-of-plane paths, and ellipse-family restriction.
The phrase fits real data well overstates a standards-consistency comparison with no independent dataset.
A degenerate negative result is retained and used to justify restoring collision loss.
All six local coefficients are reported before qualitative importance claims.
The paper names staged modeling as a strength and omitted rotation, fixed path and family restriction as separate limitations.

visualization_observations.summary: Aligned small multiples reveal circle-radius response and boundary behavior with fixed inputs shown in-panel.
Paired Et-a and Et-b plots clearly distinguish an interior a peak from monotone b behavior.
Six compact sensitivity curves expose sign, nonlinearity, and relative response.
A 3D sketch and repeated response-curve grammar help connect geometry to model stages.
Both captions are copied from Figure 17 and misdescribe the plotted slope relationships, breaking decision traceability.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: C only: the polished summary, broad coverage, and clear progression may have made the entry easy to evaluate; no official commentary establishes this.
C only: the general friction-energy ODE and analytical-to-numerical ladder may have signaled mathematical ambition despite later defects.
C only: numerous interpretable response curves and quantitative sensitivities may have strengthened perceived completeness.
C only: explicit safety, construction, and athlete-performance discussion may have offset incomplete quantitative closure.
C only: a candid limitations section may have increased credibility, but award status is not correctness evidence.

weaknesses.summary: Final energy is not equivalent to maximum vertical air without takeoff direction and airborne trajectory.
The printed landing velocity is dimensionally wrong; the correct expression is sqrt(2g(h-y0)) sin(theta).
x0 is treated as external although course shape and flight should determine it.
Forward Euler has no convergence study and bisection is unexplained for a nonmonotone two-variable objective.
b*=h0 is a boundary choice, not an interior optimized semi-axis.
Linear drag is physically dubious in the likely Reynolds-number regime and alpha is not athlete-calibrated.
The printed sensitivity coefficient uses A/B instead of B/A and is not dimensionless.
The prose claims a* increases with hi while the figure and coefficient show it decreases.
The coordinate transform mixes downhill distance and slope components inconsistently and fixes longitudinal advance externally.
Copied captions identify the wrong variables and model comparison.
Theoretical slope maximizes neither vertical air nor twist; it enforces equal initial and final hanging height.
The final 17.5-degree value is the cited real-world value written back into the recommendation, weakening independent validation.
Impact shock proportional to cos(theta) and related safety claims lack impulse, compliance, and injury modeling.
Twist remains qualitative with no angular impulse, momentum, posture, rotation, opening, or landing model.
No direct vertical-air, twist, landing, safety, construction, or tradeoff output closes the official tasks.

independent_extensions.title: Correct and test the energy solver
independent_extensions.procedure: Correct Equation 6, implement circle and ellipse cases in one solver, compare the circle numerical result with Equation 13, refine spatial step and integrator order, and publish residual and convergence tables.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Restores dimensional consistency and establishes numerical accuracy against an analytical baseline.

independent_extensions.title: Endogenize flight and landing
independent_extensions.procedure: Propagate takeoff position and velocity through projectile or aerodynamic flight, detect the first valid trajectory-course intersection, and feed the resulting impact state into the collision model.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Computes official vertical air and removes the externally fixed landing point.

independent_extensions.title: Use a constrained shape optimization
independent_extensions.procedure: Optimize splines or clothoids under width, depth, endpoint tangent, curvature, load, contact, minimum-feature, and construction constraints; classify boundary solutions and report Pareto alternatives.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Replaces degenerate and mislabeled boundary optima with buildable, traceable alternatives.

independent_extensions.title: Model twist and landing
independent_extensions.procedure: Calibrate takeoff linear and angular impulse, propagate center-of-mass flight and posture-dependent inertia, reserve opening time, and evaluate trajectory-surface intersection and landing load.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Turns the qualitative twist discussion into a testable performance and safety output.

independent_extensions.title: Replace heuristic safety with risk metrics
independent_extensions.procedure: Model normal impact speed, compliance, stopping time, peak and integrated load, departure probability, athlete heterogeneity, and construction tolerance across edge and slope angles.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Creates an auditable bridge from geometry to risk instead of relying on unsupported cosine claims.

candidate_rule_impacts.rationale: Shows why a proxy and steady-cycle criterion must be distinguished from the official unit-bearing objective.
Broad narrative coverage does not replace output-level closure of maximum air, twist, and practical tradeoffs.
Documents boundary-optimum language, figure-prose contradiction, and unsupported fit claims.
Separates useful mechanism ablation from uncalibrated parameters, unreproducible interpolation, and circular external agreement.
Adds an explicit normalization error and demonstrates the limits of one-at-a-time local curves.
The paper usefully separates theory from practical concerns but does not quantify the bridge assumptions.
Equation, solver, optimizer, coordinate, caption, and interpolation defects block end-to-end reproduction.
Adds an ODE case where unit checks, analytic comparison, and spatial convergence are all necessary.
Strong navigation, staged exposition, visual grammar, and self-critique provide a second source for the audience contract.
Adds boundary, trajectory-coupling, coordinate, and objective failures in half-pipe path design.
Provides a strong mechanism ladder while exposing regime and calibration failures in air drag.
Adds direct evidence that energy and airtime cannot replace trajectory, twist, and landing dynamics.
Shows both the value of aligned response curves and the traceability damage from copied captions and missing uncertainty.
The qualitative stomp-and-waist account illustrates the missing calibrated angular-impulse pathway.
A dedicated optimization-verification rule is needed for feasible sets, algorithm semantics, boundary classification, convergence, and decision stability.

unresolved_questions: What exact bisection or coordinate-search algorithm produced the ellipse values?
What raw data and interpolation settings produced the 17.1-degree spline intersection?
Were the reported sensitivity numbers computed from the correct B/A elasticity despite the printed Equation 16?
How were Figures 7-19 generated, and can the circle analytic result reproduce the same solver?
Did the original team have unsubmitted code or data that would resolve the convergence and calibration gaps?
No official judge commentary is available, so causal explanations for the Outstanding award remain conjectural.
